content: 1. The implementation of HCV self-testing (HCVST) should be supported by the development of standard operating procedures and training manuals tailored to the needs of the program. 2. National regulatory frameworks and policies for in vitro diagnostics (IVDs) should be reviewed to remove barriers to the availability of quality-assured HCVST products. This includes ensuring that national registration processes are streamlined and accessible. 3. WHO-prequalified products and collaborative registration procedures can be utilized to expedite the national registration of HCVST products, ensuring timely access to quality-assured diagnostics. 4. Procurement, logistics, and supply chain solutions must be carefully considered to ensure the efficient distribution of HCVST kits. 5. Community engagement is essential throughout the design, implementation, and monitoring of HCVST programs. This includes creating context-specific messages, information materials, resources, and job aids to support the program. 6. Demand generation activities, such as social marketing and promotion, should be employed to raise awareness and encourage the use of HCVST. Mobilizing staff, including peers and lay workers, is critical to supporting implementation. 7. Resource considerations should include the availability of human and financial resources to ensure the sustainable implementation of HCVST programs. 8. Service delivery models should be designed to match the needs of the target populations, considering factors such as the intended users, distribution sites, timing, and methods of kit distribution. 9. A minimum support package for self-testers should be defined, including options for in-person, virtual, or hotline-based assistance during and after self-testing. 10. Efficient referral pathways must be developed to ensure confirmatory testing and linkage to prevention, treatment, and care services for individuals with reactive HCVST results. 11. Training for providers and distributors is essential, and integration with other services, such as HIV self-testing programs, may reduce costs and improve efficiency. 12. Data collection systems should be established to monitor and evaluate HCVST programs. Indicators and data sources should be carefully selected to assess program effectiveness and inform ongoing improvements. 13. Strategies to mitigate risks, harms, and adverse events associated with HCVST should be implemented, including appropriate messaging and harm monitoring systems. 14. Regular data reviews should be conducted to refine programs and optimize implementation, ensuring alignment with national goals. 15. Distribution of HCVST kits should include clear instructions for use and materials to support correct usage and appropriate follow-up actions. These materials should also address potential misuse or harm, such as coercive testing or discrimination. 16. Community members, lay providers, and peers can play a role in developing and disseminating messages to raise awareness and encourage appropriate use of HCVST. 17. Post-market surveillance systems may need to be established or adapted to identify and report product issues or adverse events related to HCVST. 18. Existing policy frameworks and strategies for HIV self-testing can be leveraged to accelerate the introduction and scale-up of HCVST programs. 19. Service delivery approaches for HCVST should be tailored to the local context, disease burden, and community preferences. Offering a variety of models and test kit types (e.g., oral fluid and blood-based) may improve uptake. 20. Online and digital distribution models, such as home delivery or in-person collection via websites, social media, or apps, can reach populations that do not use conventional services. These models may be particularly attractive to younger individuals and key populations. 21. Facility-based distribution can occur through public and private viral hepatitis services, HIV testing services, or harm reduction programs. Secondary distribution to partners or social contacts can also be considered. 22. Community-based distribution during campaigns, events, or mobile outreach can improve access, particularly in underserved areas. Integration with existing community-based testing programs can enhance efficiency. 23. Workplace and faith-based distribution models may be useful in high HCV burden settings. 24. Many individuals can self-test accurately using manufacturer instructions, but some may require additional support. Support options should be tailored to community needs and preferences, including in-person, virtual, or hotline-based assistance. 25. Peer support models may be particularly effective for first-time testers or vulnerable populations, such as those with low literacy or disabilities. 26. Effective linkage to prevention, treatment, and care services after self-testing is critical. Clear referral pathways should be established for confirmatory testing and follow-up care. 27. Programs should monitor and evaluate HCVST implementation, including outcomes and impact, through routine data collection and operational research. 28. Voluntary self-reporting via digital platforms can provide additional insights into HCVST use, results, and linkage to care. 29. National surveys and sales data from private sector providers can help track access, availability, and trends in HCVST use. 30. Adverse events, though rare, should be monitored, reported, and addressed. Community health workers, pharmacists, and peer-led organizations can play key roles in supporting program monitoring. 31. Operational research should focus on optimizing product design, service delivery models, and linkage pathways to improve the effectiveness and scalability of HCVST programs. 32. Integration of HCVST into existing self-care programs, such as HIV self-testing, should be explored to enhance efficiency and reach. 33. Costing and budget impact analyses are necessary to plan for high-impact scale-up of HCVST programs within national health strategies.
